title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Nine days after Moscow was abandoned, a messenger from Kutuzov arrived in Petersburg with the official news. The messenger was Michaud, a Frenchman who spoke no Russian but who was, as he said of himself, quoique étranger, russe de cœur et d'âme. *
* Though a foreigner, Russian in heart and soul.

The Emperor received him at once in his study at the palace on Stone Island. Michaud had never seen Moscow before the campaign and spoke no Russian, yet he was deeply moved (so he wrote) as he stood before notre très gracieux souverain * with the news that Moscow was burning, dont les flammes éclairaient sa route. *(2)
* Our most gracious sovereign.
* (2) Whose flames lit his way.
M. Michaud's grief can hardly have had the same source as the grief of Russians, but his face was so sad when he was shown into the study that the Emperor asked him at once:
"Colonel, have you brought me bad news?"
"Very bad, sire," replied Michaud, lowering his eyes and sighing. "Moscow has been abandoned."
"My ancient capital given up without a battle?" the Emperor asked quickly, his face suddenly flushing.

Michaud respectfully passed on what Kutuzov had charged him to say. It had been impossible to fight in front of Moscow. The only choice left was between losing the army along with Moscow or losing Moscow alone, and the field marshal had been forced to choose the second.
The Emperor listened in silence, without looking at Michaud.
"Has the enemy entered the city?" he asked.
"He has, sire, and Moscow is in ashes by now. I left it all in flames," replied Michaud in a firm tone. But when he glanced at the Emperor, he was frightened at what he had done.
The Emperor began to breathe heavily and fast, his lower lip trembled, and tears welled up at once in his fine blue eyes.
It lasted only a moment. He frowned, as if reproaching himself for his weakness, then lifted his head and spoke to Michaud in a steady voice:

"I see, Colonel, from everything that is happening, that Providence demands great sacrifices from us... I am ready to submit to His will in all things. But tell me, Michaud, how did you leave the army when it saw my ancient capital given up without a battle? Did you notice any discouragement?..."
When Michaud saw that his most gracious ruler was calm again, he grew calm too. But he was not ready at once to answer the Emperor's direct and pertinent question, which demanded a direct answer.
"Sire, will you permit me to speak frankly, as a loyal soldier should?" he asked, to gain time.
"Colonel, I always demand it," replied the Emperor. "Hide nothing from me. I want to know exactly how things stand."

"Sire!" said Michaud, with a faint, barely noticeable smile, for he had now prepared a well-turned answer. "Sire, I left the whole army, from its commanders down to the humblest soldier, without exception in a state of desperate, agonized terror..."
"What do you mean?" the Emperor interrupted, frowning sternly. "Would misfortune make my Russians lose heart?... Never!"
This was what Michaud had been waiting for, to bring out the phrase he had prepared.

"Sire," he said, with respectful playfulness, "they are afraid only that Your Majesty, in the goodness of your heart, may let yourself be talked into making peace. They are burning for the fight," declared this representative of the Russian nation, "and to prove to Your Majesty, by giving their lives, how devoted they are...."
"Ah!" said the Emperor, reassured, and with a kindly gleam in his eyes he patted Michaud on the shoulder. "You set my mind at rest, Colonel."
He bowed his head and said nothing for a while.

"Well then, go back to the army," he said, drawing himself up to his full height and addressing Michaud with a gracious and majestic gesture. "Tell our brave men, and all my good subjects wherever you go, that when I have no soldier left I will put myself at the head of my beloved nobility and my good peasants, and use the last resources of my empire. It still has more to give me than my enemies suppose," said the Emperor, growing more and more animated. "But if it should ever be ordained by Divine Providence," he went on, raising his fine eyes, shining with emotion, to heaven, "that my dynasty cease to reign on the throne of my ancestors, then, when I have used up every means in my power, I will let my beard grow down to here" (he pointed halfway down his chest) "and go and eat potatoes with the poorest of my peasants, rather than sign the disgrace of my country and of my beloved people, whose sacrifices I know how to value."

The Emperor spoke these words in an agitated voice, then suddenly turned away, as if to hide from Michaud the tears rising in his eyes, and walked to the far end of his study. He stood there a few moments, then strode back to Michaud and gripped his arm firmly below the elbow. The Emperor's mild, handsome face was flushed, and his eyes gleamed with resolve and anger.

"Colonel Michaud, do not forget what I say to you here. Perhaps one day we will remember it with pleasure... Napoleon or I," said the Emperor, touching his chest. "We can no longer reign together. I have come to know him, and he will not deceive me again...."
And the Emperor stopped, frowning.

When Michaud heard these words and saw the firm resolve in the Emperor's eyes, he — quoique étranger, russe de cœur et d'âme — was carried away at that solemn moment by all he had heard (as he used to say afterwards). He gave voice to his own feelings and to those of the Russian people, whose representative he considered himself, in these words:
"Sire!" said he. "At this moment Your Majesty is signing the glory of the nation and the salvation of Europe!"
The Emperor bowed his head and dismissed him.
